content: The text provided is a long list of references and technical notes related to drinking water quality, food additives, contaminants, and toxicological evaluations. 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) have conducted extensive evaluations on aluminum exposure from all sources, including food additives. These findings were published in the 67th report of JECFA, detailing toxicological assessments and recommendations for safe levels of exposure. (WHO Technical Report Series No. 940, 2007). 2. Pesticide residues in food were evaluated in 2006 and 2007 by the Joint FAO/WHO Meeting on Pesticide Residues (JMPR). These evaluations, focusing on toxicological aspects, were published by the WHO in Geneva, providing critical insights into the safety of pesticide residues in food. 3. The 72nd and 73rd reports of JECFA, published in 2011, focused on the evaluation of certain food additives and contaminants. These reports provided detailed toxicological assessments and established guidelines for safe consumption levels. (WHO Technical Report Series Nos. 959 and 960). 4. The safety evaluation of specific contaminants in food was prepared by JECFA during its 72nd meeting. This comprehensive report, published by WHO, spans pages 685–762 and is part of the WHO Food Additives Series 63 and FAO JECFA Monographs 8. 5. Health Canada released technical guidelines in 2013 for nitrate and nitrite levels in Canadian drinking water, emphasizing the importance of maintaining safe concentrations to protect public health. 6. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) updated its evaluations of carcinogenicity in 1987, covering volumes 1–42 of its monographs. This update provided a comprehensive review of substances and their potential cancer risks to humans. 7. The International Programme on Chemical Safety (IPCS) has published numerous concise chemical safety assessments, including reports on 1,2-dichloroethane (1995, 1998), hexachlorobenzene (1997), methyl tertiary-butyl ether (1998), and chloral hydrate (2000). These documents provide detailed toxicological profiles and safety recommendations. 8. The IPCS also evaluated N-nitrosodimethylamine (2002), 1,1-dichloroethene (2003), elemental mercury and inorganic mercury compounds (2003), and hydrogen cyanide (2004). These assessments highlight the health risks associated with these chemicals and provide guidance for safe exposure levels. 9. The United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) has issued health advisories and toxicological reviews for various substances, including silver in drinking water (1992), barium and its compounds (2005), and arsenic (2001). These documents support the development of safe drinking water standards. 10. The United States National Research Council (USNRC) published scientific reviews on fluoride in drinking water (2006) and arsenic (2001), providing evidence-based recommendations for regulatory standards. 11. The WHO has published guidelines for drinking water quality since 1984, with updates in 1993, 2004, and 2021. These guidelines incorporate the latest scientific evidence to ensure the safety of drinking water worldwide. 12. Certain chemicals, such as amitraz, chlorobenzilate, and chlorothalonil, are excluded from guideline value derivation due to their rapid degradation in the environment or their unlikely occurrence in drinking water supplies. 13. Substances like asbestos, bromochloroacetate, and chloropicrin lack sufficient data to derive health-based guideline values. Similarly, chemicals such as cyanide and dichlorvos occur in drinking water at concentrations well below levels of health concern. 14. The WHO has determined that some pesticides, including permethrin and pirimiphos-methyl, are not recommended for direct application to drinking water due to safety concerns and the availability of alternative treatments. 15. Chemicals such as formaldehyde, glyphosate, and malathion are present in drinking water at concentrations significantly below levels of health concern, as supported by extensive toxicological data. 16. The WHO and other organizations emphasize the importance of monitoring and regulating chemical contaminants in drinking water to ensure public health safety, while also recognizing that some substances, such as iodine and iron, are not of health concern at typical concentrations found in drinking water.
